newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Catholic bishops strengthen ties to colleges.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Catholic bishops strengthen ties to colleges.

text.p: America's Catholic bishops voted on Wednesday to strengthen the religious presence at U.S. Catholic colleges and universities, but without taking control of such knotty issues as hiring, firing and tenure.

Members of the National Conference of Catholic Bishops approved a document emphasising the importance of Catholic identity at the 235 Catholic colleges and universities in the United States, where more than 635,000 students are enrolled.

Rooted in a document formulated in 1990 by Pope John Paul II, the measure allows university administrators to follow their own procedures for hiring and keeping staff "committed to the Catholic tradition or, if not Catholic, who are aware and respectful of that tradition."

The bishops set up a procedure that encourages dialogue between academic administrators and local bishops, with an eye to academic freedom and the rights of theologians that also allows bishops to speak out against teachings they feel are not in keeping with church doctrine.
However, bishops are not allowed to intervene to have faculty or staff dismissed or to have a say in whether tenure is granted or denied.

"The academic community is very pleased, they're happy with this document," said Rev. Thomas Reese of Woodstock Theological Seminary at the Catholic-chartered Georgetown University, who observed the bishops' proceedings. "Hopefully the bishop and the school can work together."
When this measure first surfaced, Reese said, there was anxiety among Catholic university presidents, based in part on fears of a reprisal in the case of theology professor Rev. Charles Curran.

Curran's license to teach was stripped by the Vatican in 1987 for his controversial views on abortion, divorce, homosexuality and premarital sex. Curran sued for breach of contract after the university tried to transfer him to another department. The university prevailed, but drew censure from the American Association of University Professors, a prominent academic group.
